RadioReach vs SubmitHub

By the RadioReach editorial team Published August 19, 2026 Reviewed August 19, 2026

These are different categories of product, and most artists should not be choosing between them. SubmitHub is a per-submission platform for reaching playlist curators, blogs and influencers, with a guaranteed response. RadioReach is a one-time contact file for pitching radio stations yourself. If your goal is streaming playlists or blog coverage, SubmitHub is built for that and RadioReach is not. If your goal is radio airplay and you want to own the relationships, the contact file fits better.

Who wrote this: RadioReach — we sell one of the products compared here. We have tried to describe the alternatives accurately and to say plainly where they are the better purchase. Competitor facts come from their own websites with access dates; where we could not verify a figure from a primary source, we say so instead of repeating it. Fact-checked 2026-08-18.

The core difference

SubmitHub sells access with a response attached: you pay per submission, a curator is obliged to listen and reply, and you learn quickly whether they want it. RadioReach sells research: you get an organized file of radio programming contacts, and everything after that — the pitch, the send, the follow-up — is yours to do, with no guarantee anyone replies at all.

That difference drives everything else. A per-submission platform has a cost that scales with every song and every target, and it caps your downside by guaranteeing a response. A contact file has a fixed cost and unlimited reuse, and it gives you no safety net whatsoever. Neither is better in the abstract.

The 29% approval figure is SubmitHub's own trailing-month number across the whole platform, and it is worth reading carefully: it is the share of submissions approved, not the share of artists who get meaningful traction. A guaranteed listen is a genuine product feature, and it is also the thing you are paying for each time.

Best for / avoid when

SubmitHub is the better buy when

  • You want playlist or blog placement rather than radio airplay.
  • You want a guaranteed response and written feedback on a specific song.
  • You are testing whether a single track lands before committing to a campaign.

Avoid SubmitHub when

  • Radio is the actual goal — it is not what the platform is organized around.
  • You release often and per-submission costs would compound across releases.
  • You want to build direct, ongoing relationships with programmers.

RadioReach is the better buy when

  • You are pitching radio and want the research phase collapsed.
  • You will reuse the same contacts across multiple releases.
  • You want to own the relationship and the inbox thread.

Avoid RadioReach when

  • You want guaranteed responses — a contact file guarantees nothing.
  • You want curator feedback on a track.
  • You do not have time to send and follow up personally. See our fit guide.

Plenty of artists reasonably use both: a submission platform for streaming and press, a contact file for radio. They are not substitutes.

Limitations of this page

We could not load SubmitHub's pricing page at the fact-check date, so no credit prices are stated here. Platform-reported statistics are self-reported by SubmitHub and not independently audited. This comparison covers structural differences rather than a head-to-head outcome test, because we have no way to run an equivalent campaign through both and measure it fairly.

Frequently asked questions

Is SubmitHub better than RadioReach?

For playlists, blogs and curator feedback, yes — that is what it is built for. For radio outreach where you want direct contact and reuse across releases, the contact file fits better. They are different categories, and the honest answer depends entirely on whether your goal is streaming placement or radio airplay.

Can I use SubmitHub to get on the radio?

Some radio curators do accept submissions there, but the platform is oriented around playlists, blogs and influencers. If radio is your primary goal, pitching stations directly reaches far more of them, including the college and community stations most open to independent artists.
